This log was generated on 2026-08-08 from the verification registries. Release checks block a figure-affecting change that lacks an entry.

Engine changelog

Figure-affecting engine changes, recorded at release

32 entries
E-32 · 2026-08-08engine release 8 August 2026
Affected: Short-term and low-value exempt leases, whose straight-line expense figures were produced and then cleared instead of shown; Leases whose term is shortened, which must now state the rent payable in the final period of the shortened term; Leases with a break option that is reasonably certain to be taken, which must now state the rent payable in the final period before the exit; Leases carrying a make-good or restoration amount, which must now state the rate used to discount that provision

A lease claiming the short-term or low-value exemption now shows its straight-line expense figures on screen, in the saved record and in the workbook. Before this change the calculator worked those figures out correctly and then discarded them, so the amount the standard requires a preparer to disclose was never visible. How the expense is worked out has not changed. This entry also records three questions the calculator now asks before it will measure a lease, which were introduced in the previous release and not written down at the time: the rent payable in the final period when a term is shortened, the rent payable in the final period before an exit under a break option, and the rate used to discount a make-good provision. A lease saved before this release that leaves any of them blank is held at the question until it is answered. No saved figure changes, and nothing is recalculated behind anyone.

Where the short-term or low-value exemption is elected, the payments are recognised as an expense on a straight-line basis over the lease term under IFRS 16.6, and IFRS 16.53 requires that expense to be disclosed. The calculator produced the figures and then cleared them before they reached the screen, the saved record or the workbook, so the preparer could not read the number they were required to report. The figures are now published. The note asking the preparer to confirm the exemption still has to be acknowledged before a workbook can be produced, and the workbook is still withheld until it is. A worked check on a twelve month lease paying five thousand a month in arrears gives twelve equal periods of five thousand and a total of sixty thousand, with the set-up costs and the termination penalty correctly excluded, because neither is a lease payment under the exemption and the term does not reflect exercising an option to terminate. THREE QUESTIONS THE CALCULATOR NOW ASKS. These were introduced in the release dated the sixth of August and were not described in the record at the time. They are recorded here so that a preparer who meets one of them knows it is deliberate. First, where a lease term is shortened, the rent payable in the final period of the shortened term must be stated. It cannot safely be assumed, because the honest answer differs by payment timing: a lease paid in arrears still owes the rent for that period, while a lease paid in advance has already paid it and owes nothing further. IFRS 16.45 requires the remaining consideration to be remeasured using the revised payments, and the revised payments are what this question establishes. Enter nought where nothing further is due. Second, the same question is asked where a break option is reasonably certain to be taken, for the period that ends at the exit. Third, where a lease carries a make-good or restoration amount, the rate used to discount that provision must be stated. A make-good obligation is measured under IAS 37 and its discount rate is a separate judgement from the rate used for the lease itself, so the calculator no longer borrows one for the other. A lease saved before this release which does not carry an answer to one of these is held at the question the next time it is opened or recalculated. Its saved figures are shown once the question is answered. No stored figure is changed and nothing is recalculated without the preparer asking for it. Separately, a calculation for a lease with no changes and no reviews recorded against it no longer carries two empty placeholder sections in its saved record. Every figure, schedule, journal and report is unchanged by that, and only the workbook built-in integrity fingerprint reflects the slimmer saved data, so no saved lease is marked as affected by it.

E-31 · 2026-08-06engine release 6 August 2026
Affected: Leases where the decision to leave is made between regular payment dates; Leases where an index change and a revised payment take effect on the same day; Leases paid quarterly or annually whose index review falls between payment dates

An early-exit decision can now use the date it was actually made, provided it is before the exit date; it no longer has to fall on a regular payment date. When an index change and a revised payment take effect on the same day, the calculator now asks whether the amount entered already includes the index change. That answer follows the lease through calculation, save and load, the chart, disclosures and the workbook, so the change is applied once rather than twice or not at all. Index reviews on quarterly and annual leases are mapped to the first contractual payment period on or after the entered date.

The early-exit path preserves the entered decision and exit dates, splits the affected accounting period at the real date and closes the liability and right-of-use asset on the chosen exit date. A same-day index review and payment-setting change cannot be calculated until the user states the contractual fact: either the revised payment already contains the current index movement or the movement must still be applied. The calculator does not try to infer that answer from whether two amounts happen to be equal. Hidden, stale or conflicting answers are rejected, and a payment change combined with a term change on the same day keeps one shared basis through the complete package. For non-monthly leases, the mapping uses the contractual payment cadence rather than a monthly shortcut. The permanent family tests cover both answers, different amounts, all payment-setting change types, multi-row changes, later index reviews, save and reload, export controls, disclosures, chart data and deliberate mutations.

E-30 · 2026-08-06engine release 6 August 2026
Affected: Leases whose right-of-use asset starts with a credit balance; Leases with more than one index review landing in the same accounting period; Leases whose index remeasurement is recorded at the end of a period

No lease balance, payment or charge changes. Where the right-of-use asset starts with a credit balance, the journal now puts positive amounts in the correct debit or credit columns instead of putting a negative amount in the opposite column. When more than one index review lands in one accounting period, the audit evidence keeps the review that was measured and lists the ignored review separately. An index remeasurement recorded at period end now appears after that period's payment and accrual, so the final journal balance agrees with the closing schedule.

The schedule and measurement results are unchanged. The journal correction covers recognition of a credit-balance right-of-use asset, its release over the applicable term and any later derecognition or owned-asset tail. The index evidence now separates the rows entered, rows moved to payment dates, the row retained for measurement and any same-period row ignored under the first-row rule. Too few or too many mapping rows both stop the workbook from being treated as clean. Period-end remeasurement is recorded as the closing event for that period, which makes the final journal carrying balance agree with the schedule without changing any underlying amount.

E-29 · 2026-08-05engine release 5 August 2026
Affected: Leases where a break or lease-term decision is made between regular payment dates; Leases with a termination penalty; Leases with a separately entered amount due at the end of the term; Leases whose revised payments start on an entered date after a change; Leases with an index remeasurement and another change on the same day or later; Leases with a restoration provision that is remeasured after commencement

Lease changes can now use the date that actually applies, even when it falls between normal payment dates. A break or early exit keeps the entered decision and exit dates, maps them to the correct accounting periods, and closes the liability and right-of-use asset on the real exit date. A termination penalty is included only when the exercised termination option and exit basis agree. Regular rent and any separate amount due at the end of the lease remain distinct and settle on their proper dates. Revised payments, index changes and restoration remeasurements now keep their entered timing and rate evidence through the schedules, journals, reconciliations and exports.

This release corrects the full date-and-event family rather than one example. Exact decision dates are accepted before the chosen break or exit date and are no longer rejected merely because they do not coincide with a normal payment boundary. The calculator preserves the entered dates in its trace, maps the remeasurement to the correct accounting period, creates the required final stub and closes the lease on the chosen exit date. Termination penalties now require one coherent exercised-option and exit-date basis before they enter the liability. Final recurring rent is kept separate from purchase-option prices, residual value guarantees, termination penalties and other end-of-term cash, so each amount appears once on its actual settlement date. A modification uses its entered first revised payment date rather than silently inheriting the original cadence. Index remeasurements and later changes keep their chronological order in the schedule and journal evidence. Restoration provision remeasurements use the entered current rate, retain that provenance through save and load, and carry the resulting right-of-use and journal movements into the reconciliation and workbook controls. The golden refresh was accepted only after a 15-scenario old-to-new comparison, an engine-independent 24-value clean-room derivation for the one monetary mixed-chain movement, and a planted one-cent mutation that the oracle rejected.

E-28 · 2026-08-03engine release 3 August 2026
Affected: Leases with two or more changes falling close together, where the schedule shows two months as a single row

No balance, charge or interest amount changes on any lease. If your lease was changed twice within a short period, the schedule shows the two months those changes span as a single row, and that row now includes the movement in value that happened between them. Before, the movement had nowhere to appear, so the row did not add up and the column that would explain a difference showed nothing. The period end shown on such a row was also the end of the earlier month rather than the later one, which disagreed with the date printed beside it on the same row and with the liability schedule. Both the liability and the right of use schedules were affected in the same way and both are corrected.

When two changes to a lease fall close together, the calculator shows the two months they span as a single row rather than as two. On that row the opening balance was already correct, the closing balance was already correct, and the depreciation charge was already correct. What was missing was the change in the carrying amount recorded between those two months. The calculator carries such a change into the following month opening balance, so on ordinary rows it is visible as a step from one row to the next. On a merged row there is no following row for it to appear in, so it was simply absent: the figures on the face of the row did not reconcile, and the column that exists to explain exactly that kind of difference read as nothing. The period end printed on a merged row was taken from the earlier of the two months rather than the later, so it disagreed with the date shown beside it on the same row, with the equivalent row on the liability schedule, and with the charge on the row itself which covered the whole span. Both schedules took their merged rows from the same place and both showed the same two problems, so both are corrected together. Nothing about how the lease is measured has changed, and no amount you have already reported moves as a result: the underlying month by month figures were correct throughout and only the merged presentation of them was wrong.

E-27 · 2026-08-03engine release 3 August 2026
Affected: Leases where you entered a date on which you received a lease incentive

No amount changes on any lease, and no interest, balance or charge is affected. If you entered a date on which you received a lease incentive, the date the workbook printed for it could be a different day from the one you typed and from the one the calculator used. It happened where the day and the month could each be read as the other, so a date typed as the fifth of June could be printed as the sixth of May. It affected leases presented in a currency whose dates are written month first, and no others. The calculator now holds that date one way everywhere, so what you typed, what it uses and what the workbook prints are the same day.

The date was being stored in a form that depended on the currency, at three separate points inside the calculator, and one of those points kept whatever separator was typed. The result was that the same day could be held in two different ways at once, and the workbook wrote one of them into a real date cell while the calculation had used the other. Measured across a corpus of leases, four in every hundred were affected: every one of them presented in a currency written month first with a day and month that could be swapped, and none at all in any other currency or with any unambiguous date. If you hold a workbook for a lease with an incentive receipt date, open the Inputs tab and compare the receipt date row against what you entered. Exporting that lease again after this change gives a workbook that agrees with your entry.

E-26 · 2026-08-03engine release 3 August 2026
No user-visible figure changes

No figure changes anywhere, on any lease, and nothing already calculated or exported needs redoing. The right-of-use schedule now states the period each row covers, in the same way the lease liability schedule already did. Those two columns had been showing as empty on every row of the right-of-use table, so you could read the balances but not see which month an opening balance belonged to. No date was ever wrong, and the date already shown beside each row was and remains correct.

The right-of-use table on the results page offers a period start and a period end beside every row. Until now the calculator did not supply either, so both columns were blank for the whole of every lease while the same two columns on the lease liability table were filled in. The two schedules are built from one set of monthly periods, so describing that set on one table and not the other left a reader with no way to check an opening balance against the month it belongs to. The commencement row deliberately shows no period on both tables, because it records a single instant rather than a span of time. Nothing about how any amount is worked out has changed, and a schedule saved before today opens exactly as it did.

E-25 · 2026-08-01engine release 1 August 2026
No user-visible figure changes

No figure changes anywhere, on any lease, and nothing already calculated or exported needs redoing. Where the calculator writes a date into a sentence for you to read, it now names the month. A note explaining that an index review has been moved to the nearest payment date used to give both dates as digits only, so the sentence explaining a date change was itself readable two ways, and a reader in one country could take it to mean a different month from a reader in another. Those sentences now say the month in words. The dates the calculator stores, compares and puts in the schedule are untouched, because other parts of the workbook read them back and match them exactly.

This is a wording change and only a wording change. Every figure on every schedule, every balance and every journal line is identical before and after, checked across a corpus of leases covering different start dates, payment frequencies, currencies and timings, down to the last digit a computer can represent. The reason the engine version has moved at all is that your browser keeps a copy of the calculator until the version changes; without a new version a returning visitor would keep seeing the old sentences.

E-24 · 2026-08-01engine release 27 July 2026
No user-visible figure changes

No figure changed anywhere, on any lease, and nothing already calculated or exported is affected. This changes only how our own internal test system takes a fingerprint of a result so it can tell whether anything has moved since last time.

The fingerprint used to be taken to a fixed number of decimal places. On a lease of several hundred thousand that worked out finer than a computer can reproduce the same arithmetic twice on two different machines, so the same lease could fingerprint two different ways depending on where the check ran. The figures were identical; only the very last digits, far beyond a cent, differed. The fingerprint is now taken to a number of meaningful digits instead, chosen by measurement over nine hundred leases and more than four million individual figures so that it still notices a change of a thousandth of a currency unit while ignoring differences no arithmetic can reproduce. Every recorded fingerprint was retaken, which is why they all differ from the previous release, and every one of the checks that compare actual amounts stayed green throughout, which is what shows no figure moved.

E-23 · 2026-07-27engine release 27 July 2026
Affected: Leases where the rent is paid in advance

On a lease where the rent is paid in advance, the journal now dates each period's interest and depreciation to the end of the period they belong to. They used to be dated the first day of the following period. No amount has changed and no balance has changed. What changes is which month, and in some cases which financial year, an expense falls into. The clearest effect is on the very first month: a lease starting on 1 January previously showed no interest and no depreciation at all for January, even though the asset was in use from day one. It now shows both, dated 31 January. Leases where the rent is paid in arrears were always dated correctly and are unaffected.

Interest is a charge for each period the lease liability is outstanding, and depreciation runs from the commencement date, so both belong to the period the schedule row covers. Paying in advance changes the balance the interest is calculated on, which the calculator already handled correctly, but it does not move the period the expense falls into. The old rule was also inconsistent with itself: the final period has no following period, so it fell back to its own period end, meaning a single lease used two different rules. Because the dates moved, a saved schedule re-rendered today will show these rows on different dates from a copy exported before this change, and the calculator will tell you so. The amounts on those rows are identical. Two related things were corrected at the same time. The check that verifies journal dates was expecting exactly what the calculator was producing, so it agreed with the error and never reported it; it now takes its expectation from the schedule independently. And on leases priced in US dollars the journal was not listed in date order, because the dates were being read back in a different format from the one they were written in, which pushed every period-end row to the bottom of the list.

E-21 · 2026-07-26engine release 26 July 2026
No user-visible figure changes

No figure changes anywhere, on any lease, and nothing already exported was miscalculated by this. It closes a way the calculator could have gone wrong quietly in future rather than fixing something it was doing wrong today. When the schedule is built, two payment entries can in principle compete for the same month, and only the earlier one is used. On every input we can construct that situation never arises, and it did not arise across six thousand test leases. But if it ever did, the amount that lost would simply have vanished from the schedule while the amount you owe had already been measured on it, so the schedule would quietly pay less than the lease says and the closing balance would not reach nil, with nothing anywhere telling you. The row now records what was set aside, so it can never happen without being visible. An adversary checking this work found the same hole one step further along, where an entry carries no interest cost but does carry cash, and that is closed in the same change.

Two claims in the code comments were checked by measurement and both were wrong, so they are corrected here rather than left to mislead. The first said the situation arises after a mid-month shortening of the term; three hundred and seventy eight scenarios produced none. The second said sharing a calendar month cannot mean sharing a schedule slot; over three hundred and sixty runs, two pairs shared both. What actually keeps this from arising is an earlier step that merges the payment streams and removes the duplicate before the schedule is built. The choice to keep the earlier entry is also not required by the standard, which says nothing about one payment per period; it is right because the entry that loses is an artefact of merging two streams rather than a second amount the lease makes payable, and if a genuine second amount ever arrived the recording is what would make it visible.

E-20 · 2026-07-26engine release 26 July 2026
No user-visible figure changes

No figure changes anywhere, on any lease, and nothing already exported was miscalculated by this. What changes is whether the audit pack will sign off when one of the index rows you entered could not be used. Where the same index review date was entered twice carrying two different readings, the calculator used the first one you typed and the pack came out signed off with nothing raised, so neither you nor a reviewer had anything to work from. Only you can say which of the two readings is right, so the pack now refuses to sign off and names both of them, which row each came from, and which one the figures were measured on. An index reading below zero dated inside the lease term behaved the same way and is now treated the same way. Where the same date appears twice with the same reading there is nothing to resolve and nothing changes. A reading dated outside the lease term still cannot change any figure of that lease, so it does not stop you signing off, but it is now listed so you can see that a row you entered was not used. The user facing account of this, and what to do if you have such a lease, is recorded in the corrections register for the same date.

The problem was not in the index calculation, which was right throughout. Whenever a lease carried anything in its modification section the whole lease was rebuilt in date order, and that rebuild started the list of things needing your attention empty while every other record of the ignored rows survived. Because the audit pack grades its exceptions from that one list, each layer looked correct when checked on its own, which is why the existing checks passed. The list is now carried across the rebuild for the rows whose meaning cannot change, and re-derived from the rebuild for the one that can, because a modification is able to move the end date and a row that fell outside the original term may sit inside the revised one.

E-19 · 2026-07-26engine release 26 July 2026
Affected: Leases with a purchase option you are reasonably certain to exercise, where the asset's useful life ends before the lease does, and something happens after the right-of-use asset has already been written down in full

This finishes off the change published immediately before it, and it corrects the running balances the journal reports rather than any amount charged. On the leases in that same class, where the write-down of the right-of-use asset ends before the lease does and something later increases what you owe, the charge that the earlier change introduced was carrying blank balances alongside it. The period it landed in closed on a journal line reporting nothing owed, when in the case we measured a quarter of a million was still owed and the lease liability schedule said so. And although accumulated depreciation was credited with the charge, the accumulated depreciation balance the journal reported did not move, so for the rest of the lease it was short by exactly the amount that had been charged. On the lease we measured that was 17,068.53 short from the seventh year to the end. Nothing you pay, nothing charged to profit or loss and nothing on the liability or right-of-use schedules moves. What changes is that the journal now reports the amount owed and the accumulated depreciation that it has itself recorded.

The charge in question was modelled on the line the calculator already writes at the very bottom of a purchase-option lease, where the asset is still being written down after the lease itself has ended. That line reports the lease liability as nothing, and it is telling the truth, because by then the lease has finished and nothing is owed. This new charge lands in the middle of the lease instead, while rent is still being paid and interest is still accruing, and it took the shape without the truth. The two figures it reported were therefore not wrong arithmetic but a blank where a balance belongs. Both are now read from the period the charge falls in. Because the charge is posted part way through the lease, every later line has to carry it as well, or the balance the journal reports stops agreeing with the depreciation the journal has itself recorded and stays wrong to the end of the lease. Those later lines now carry it. The reason this matters even though no amount you pay or charge has moved is that the journal keeps its own balances, built separately from the schedules, and that is exactly what makes it worth having as a second opinion. A line that fills a balance in with a blank instead of the figure in force turns that second opinion into something made up. It is worth saying plainly that this was reachable only through the journal's own balance columns. The workbook and the on-screen journal show the entries themselves rather than these running balances, so nothing you have already exported or printed showed a wrong figure because of it. The correction is nonetheless published because the balances are part of what the calculator reports. The class was swept rather than the reported case patched: every journal line across the whole test population was checked for a movement recorded against a balance that did not move by it, and there are none left. Two other kinds of line were found carrying the same kind of blank, the one that records receipt of a lease incentive and the one that records a new estimate of a make-good obligation, but neither is ever the line that closes its period, so neither is ever read as the balance a period ends on. That is recorded here rather than quietly changed, because widening the correction to cover them would have altered leases where nothing is actually reported wrongly. The answer was anchored outside the calculator, on the rule that over a whole lease the asset and the liability both start and end at nothing, so what reaches profit or loss over the life has to equal what leaves the bank. That figure was worked out from the rent, the index uplift and the option price with the calculator switched off, and it is unchanged before and after, which is how we know a balance moved and an amount did not.

E-18 · 2026-07-25engine release 25 July 2026
Affected: Leases with a purchase option you are reasonably certain to exercise, where the asset's useful life ends before the lease does, and something happens after the right-of-use asset has already been written down in full

When you are reasonably certain you will buy the asset at the end, the right-of-use asset is written down over the asset's own useful life rather than over the lease term, which is what IFRS 16.32 asks for. If the life you have entered ends before the lease does, the write-down finishes early and the lease carries on without it. Anything that then increased what you owe was being added to the right-of-use asset and then charged nowhere at all, because that asset's own schedule had already finished and had no period left to put it in. The amount sat on the balance sheet for good and the cost never reached profit or loss. It is now charged in the period the change happens, because the write-down period the standard sets has already run out by then, so there is nothing left to spread it over. Seven kinds of change were affected and every one of them is fixed: a review of an index, a rent review, a longer term, a shorter term, more space, less space, and a new estimate of a make-good obligation. On a six-year lease with a three and a half year useful life the amounts we measured ranged from 14,869.16 on a reduction in space to 180,193.07 on a reassessment that extended the term. A reduction in what you owe already behaved correctly and is unchanged.

Two paragraphs pull in opposite directions here and both of them apply. IFRS 16.39 says a remeasurement of the lease liability is recognised as an adjustment to the right-of-use asset, and the only exception it gives is for a further reduction once the asset is already at nil, which is not what an increase is. So the amount does belong on the asset, and the entry that put it there was right. What was missing was the other half. IFRS 16.31 applies the depreciation requirements of IAS 16 to the asset, and IFRS 16.32 has already fixed the period for a purchase-option lease at the asset's useful life, so once that life has passed there is no remaining period and the whole amount falls into the period it arises in. The asset goes back to nil in the same period it is recognised, which is where it already was, so nothing you see on the right-of-use schedule changes. What changes is that the cost now reaches profit or loss instead of disappearing. A useful life that ends before the lease does is an unusual thing to enter, since being reasonably certain you will buy an asset and expecting it to be finished before you own it do not sit comfortably together, so it is worth checking the life is the one you meant. Nothing about a lease without a purchase option changes, nothing changes where the life you entered covers the whole term, and nothing changes where the review lands while the write-down is still running. The opposite direction was already right and stays as it is: where a change reduces what you owe after the asset has reached nil, the reduction goes straight to profit or loss under the second sentence of IFRS 16.39, and it did so to the cent before this change and still does. Two published sources reach the same place from different directions and both were read in full before being relied on. A Big Four guide says that where a change is added to the right-of-use asset it is then written down over that asset's remaining useful life, which where none is left can only mean it is charged at once. And IFRIC 1 paragraph 7, which covers a change in a make-good obligation rather than a lease liability, says in terms that once the related asset has reached the end of its useful life all subsequent changes in the obligation are recognised in profit or loss as they occur. That is a different obligation under a different standard so it is not authority here, but it is the same problem answered the same way, and worth knowing about if you are documenting the treatment. The fix was checked against every kind of change the calculator accepts rather than only the one that was reported, and against a figure worked out from the rent, the index uplift and the option price with the calculator switched off, on the principle that over the whole life of a lease what you charge has to equal what you pay.

E-17 · 2026-07-25engine release 25 July 2026
Affected: Leases with an index or rent review that was overtaken by a later change to the lease; Leases with a landlord contribution still to be received when the lease was changed

Corrected how the calculator treats an index or rent review that was overtaken by a later change to the lease. Where a lease was paid in advance on a quarterly or annual cycle, carried a review whose reviewed rent had not yet fallen due, and was then changed so that rent was paid in arrears, the schedule and the journals could tell different stories about the same lease, and the lease could finish with a balance still showing after every contractual payment had been made.

The liability schedule was rebuilt from a point earlier than the change, which discarded the remeasurement the change itself had already produced. On a three year lease with nothing but rent this left more than eighteen hundred of liability outstanding at the end. On a larger lease with several changes it reached more than seventy five thousand, and it grew in proportion to the size of the lease. The workbook’s own liability check reported the schedule and the journals a long way apart, so the figures disagreed in a way a reviewer would see but could not explain. A lease liability is carried at amortised cost, so a balance measured as the present value of the payments still to come, then increased by the interest on it and reduced by exactly those payments, is extinguished by the end of the lease. That is now true of every lease of this shape. The same correction settles what happens to the review itself. A lease liability is remeasured for an index or rate change only when there is a change in the cash flows, which is when the adjustment to the lease payments takes effect. Where a lease change replaced the rent before the reviewed rent was next due, no payment was ever made at the reviewed level, so there is nothing to remeasure. The calculator no longer lifts the newly agreed rent by that earlier review, and it now says on the workbook that the review had no effect and why, rather than leaving that to be inferred from the figures. A review dated after the change still applies to the rent then in force, exactly as before. A separate correction in the same change fixes the month a landlord contribution still to be received is recorded in, when a lease change switches the rent between payment in advance and payment in arrears. The receipt now follows the arrangement that applied on the date it fell due, so a change made afterwards no longer moves it a month and no longer restates periods that had already closed. Only leases of these shapes move, and every one of them was already showing a lease that did not close. No lease outside them changes by a cent. Where a saved schedule is affected the drift notice will say so, and in these cases it is telling you something you need to see. References: IFRS 16 paragraph 36, a lease liability is carried at amortised cost. Paragraph 42 sub-paragraph b, remeasure for an index or rate change only when the adjustment to the lease payments takes effect. Paragraph 45, a change that is not a separate lease is accounted for at its effective date using the revised payments and a revised discount rate.

E-16 · 2026-07-25engine release 25 July 2026
No user-visible figure changes

A maintenance change to the frozen example set, with no change to any figure. The frozen examples are how we notice when a release moves a number, and they were being replayed through a shortcut into the calculation rather than through the calculation the website actually runs. The shortcut skips five things the real one does, including the whole treatment of a short-term exempt lease and the reassessment that applies when a break is reasonably certain, so an example written for either of those was quietly frozen against an ordinary lease instead and would have matched for ever while watching nothing. Two such examples had already been written and thrown away for that reason. Every example now replays through the same path a person using the calculator goes through, three more have been added for the classes that were unreachable, and every one of them now has to prove it engages the case it is named for or it fails by name. Nothing a user could have seen changes.

Three things were found while making the change, and each is worth recording because none of them was visible before. First, an example that carried a make-good obligation or a rent-free opening was declaring that input under a name the real calculation does not accept, so through the real path the lease being frozen did not have the feature on it at all. Every example is now checked against the list of inputs the real calculation accepts, read from the calculation itself rather than kept by hand, and one that declares an input the calculation would drop fails by name. Second, attaching a later change to a lease that has already been through the real calculation and come back as data behaves differently from attaching it inside the calculation: on a rent or scope change it visibly does nothing, and on a term reassessment it looks completely correct while spreading the extension back to the start of the lease instead of applying it at the reassessment date. Later changes are therefore now passed in with the lease, the way the website passes them, and the checks that would have missed that are recorded. Third, one example was checking the reassessed end date against a field the real calculation deliberately overwrites with the date the user typed, so it is now checked against the reassessed date the calculation reports and against the length of the lease after the reassessment, both of which can be worked out from the dates alone. A known limit is recorded alongside the set: the running balance of a make-good provision is not part of what the real calculation returns, so the examples watch the yearly unwinding and the re-estimated amount instead, which are.

E-15 · 2026-07-25engine release 25 July 2026
Affected: Leases where the landlord contribution is received after the lease starts

A landlord contribution that is agreed at the start of a lease but paid later now reduces the lease liability, at present value, instead of being taken off the right-of-use asset in full on day one. IFRS 16.27(a) measures the liability from the lease payments less any lease incentives receivable, while IFRS 16.24(b) takes off the right-of-use cost only the incentives received. Those are different words doing different work, and the calculator was applying the second rule to both cases. The clearest sign was that changing the date the money arrives moved no figure at all. It moves several now. On one measured lease, sixty monthly payments of 12,000 at 5.5 per cent with a contribution of 30,000 arriving three months in, the opening liability falls from 630,272.25 to 600,671.13, the opening right-of-use asset rises from 600,272.25 to 600,671.13, and total interest over the life of the lease falls from 89,727.75 to 89,328.87. Moving that same contribution out to three years in gives an opening liability of 605,063.54, where before it gave 630,272.25 whatever date you entered. Total cash over the life of the lease is unchanged, and so is total profit or loss: what moves is the balance sheet and the split between interest and depreciation.

The contribution is now treated as what the standard calls it, a lease payment with a negative sign, so it is discounted on the same basis as the rent and it sits in the schedule until the money actually arrives. Three consequences follow. There is no longer a separate gross receivable on the balance sheet at the start of the lease, because the amount is already inside the liability at present value and showing it twice would overstate both sides. The receipt is journalled against the lease liability rather than against a receivable, in the period the schedule steps in, so the journals and the schedule agree. And where the contribution arrives in a month that also carries rent, both entries are now posted: the net movement in that month can be negative, and the rule that decided whether to post the rent was reading that net figure, so the rent entry and its cash were being dropped. Later events carry the contribution too. An index or rate review, a rent change, a scope change, a term change and a make-good re-estimate all rebuild the payment schedule, and each of them was either losing an unpaid contribution altogether or, on the index path, uplifting it as though a fixed amount agreed with the landlord moved with inflation. A contribution still to be received is now included in the remeasured liability at present value, and because it is a fixed contractual amount rather than an index linked one, a review revises the rent and leaves the contribution alone. One case is worth stating plainly because it looks wrong at first glance. Where the contribution is larger than the rent still due before it arrives, the lease liability shows as a negative amount for the months in between. That is the arithmetic of the standard rather than a fault, it is always temporary, and it always closes on the receipt. The calculator produces those figures, explains them in plain English naming both amounts, and keeps the workbook flagged for review rather than signing it off. Refusing to calculate would have been worse: the same economics are already accepted when the identical contribution is received on day one, so refusing this one would accept or reject the same lease on the strength of the cheque date alone.

E-14 · 2026-07-25engine release 25 July 2026
Affected: Leases with an index or rate review where the rent is paid at the end of each period; Leases with an index or rate review where the rent is paid at the start of each period

An index or rate review is now recognised in the period that contains the date it takes effect, and the revised rent now starts with the first period that begins on or after that date. On a lease paid at the end of each period, a review dated on a payment date used to raise that period rent even though the payment was for occupancy the lessee had already had, so the total cash over the life of the lease was overstated by one uplift. And because the schedule could only show a step by resetting the next period opening balance, a review taking effect on 31 December was reported in the following January. IFRS 16.42(b) remeasures a lease liability only when there is a change in the cash flows, meaning when the adjustment to the lease payments takes effect, and it determines the revised payments for the remainder of the lease term. Those are two different questions, and on a lease paid at the end of each period they are meant to be able to resolve to two different dates. On one measured lease with a review taking effect on 31 December 2028, December rent goes back to the contractual 11,000 from 12,100, total cash over the life of the lease falls from 687,500.00 to 686,400.00, the year interest falls from 16,896.75 to 16,780.64, the year depreciation from 116,588.46 to 115,549.91, and the right-of-use asset at 31 December 2028 rises from 256,025.02 to 256,079.67. The lease liability at that date is 274,778.29 both before and after, because the two errors happened to cancel on that one figure, which is worth saying plainly rather than letting an unchanged number suggest nothing was wrong.

Three smaller corrections travel with it. The liability schedule and the right-of-use schedule each gained a remeasurement column, so the step can be shown in the period it belongs to and every row still adds up on its face, with the closing balance carrying straight into the next opening balance. The column appears only on a lease that actually has a review, so every other schedule and every other export is unchanged to the cell. Under IFRS 16.39 the right-of-use asset moves by the same amount as the lease liability, and it does here to the cent. Second, the remeasurement journal now carries the same date as the balance step it explains. It could previously sit up to a month away, and on the very example this calculator had been treating as its control, the balance stepped on 31 January while the journal was dated 28 February, putting a journal and the balance it explains in different months. Third, an index review that takes effect on or after the start of the final payment period is now reported rather than disappearing. No remaining payment can be charged at the revised rent, so nothing in the schedule changes and that is correct, but the total cash over the life of the lease used to fall by a full uplift with nothing said about it. It is now shown as something to check, and it does not stop the calculation, because the arithmetic is right and a review can legitimately land there. Where a review takes effect part way through a period, the step is shown at that period closing rather than on the exact day. That is a stated choice rather than a requirement, no published guidance addresses the part way case, and it changes no balance sheet figure because every reporting date falls on a period boundary.

E-13 · 2026-07-25engine release 25 July 2026
No user-visible figure changes

A maintenance change to the frozen example set, with no change to any figure. The frozen examples are how we notice when a release moves a number, and the set had grown narrow: none of the eight carried a lease incentive, an amount owed at the end of the term, a purchase option, a break option, a fixed rent escalation, initial direct costs or a rent-free opening period, so several recent releases moved no frozen figure at all. Three more examples were added, covering initial direct costs with a rent-free opening and a yearly escalation, an amount owed at the end of the term on a lease paid in advance, and a purchase option whose asset life is shorter than the lease. Nothing a user could have seen changes.

Two further examples were written and deliberately left out, which matters more than the three that stayed. A short-term exempt lease and a break option that becomes reasonably certain were both prepared, and both turned out to be frozen against an ordinary lease rather than the case they were named for, because of how the replay reaches the calculation. Each one carries a check derived from its own dates rather than from the calculator, and those checks caught it: the exempt example reported no exempt term at all, and the break example reported the full eight years where the exit date says six. They were removed rather than published, and both cases stay covered by the release-to-release comparisons instead. Two classes are also deliberately not frozen yet, an incentive received after the lease starts and how an index reading dated on a period end is applied, because corrections to both are in progress and freezing a figure now would make it impossible to say later whether it moved because of the correction or because of the freeze. Every reason and the condition that lifts it is recorded alongside the example set.

E-12 · 2026-07-25engine release 25 July 2026
Affected: Leases with a termination penalty where the early exit becomes reasonably certain after the lease starts; The reassessment adjustment reported when a lease with a termination penalty is shortened to its exit date; Leases where the confirmation that the end date is an early exit now changes the opening liability, not only the warnings

A termination penalty is no longer added to the opening lease liability when the early exit only becomes reasonably certain after the lease has started. It now enters the figures at the reassessment, on the shortened term, at the revised rate. Under IFRS 16.27(e) a termination penalty belongs in the lease liability only if the lease term reflects the lessee exercising an option to terminate, and where the exit is entered as a break at a date earlier than the end date, the term at the start of the lease still runs to the end date, so it does not yet reflect that exit. On one measured lease the opening liability was overstated by 186,814.54, which is 28.56 per cent, and the adjustment reported at the reassessment was shown as a decrease of 88,115.21 when it is in fact an increase of 134,383.90. The whole amount is still in the figures and the lifetime cash is unchanged: this is a correction to when the penalty is recognised, not whether it is. Leases where you have confirmed that the end date itself is the early exit are unchanged to the cent, and so is every lease without a termination penalty.

IFRS 16.27(e) includes payments of penalties for terminating a lease in the lease payments only if the lease term reflects the lessee exercising an option to terminate. IFRS 16.18(b) and the definition of the lease term include an optional period unless the lessee is reasonably certain to end the lease, and IFRS 16.20 requires the term to be reassessed when a significant event or change in circumstances arises. IFRS 16.40(a) then requires the revised lease payments to be determined on the basis of the revised lease term, and IFRS 16.41 sets the rate used at that point. Where the exit is entered as a break option at a date earlier than the end date, those paragraphs read together mean the penalty sits outside the opening measurement and enters at the reassessment, on the shortened term, at the revised rate. The calculator previously added the penalty at the start of the lease on the strength of the amount alone, and at the same time treated the presence of the break as reason enough to stay silent about the contradiction, so the one situation where the conflict was real was the one situation the calculator did not mention. Three further points, stated plainly because each changes what you see. First, if the break cannot be applied at all, for example because it overlaps a change to the lease, the penalty stays in the opening measurement exactly as before and the calculator raises the coherence note instead, so no amount you entered is ever dropped. Second, confirming that the end date is itself the early exit now affects the opening liability and not only the warnings, because that confirmation means the term already reflects the termination. Third, if you both confirm the end date as the exit and enter a break on a different date, the calculator now tells you that those are two different exit dates for the same lease, keeps your figures as they are, and asks you to resolve which date is the exit rather than changing a measurement on your behalf.

E-11 · 2026-07-25engine release 25 July 2026
Affected: Leases where an incentive received at or before the start of the lease is larger than the rest of the cost of the right-of-use asset, so the asset starts below nil; Leases where a later reduction in the lease liability brings the right-of-use asset down to nil, whether that reduction comes from an index review, a change to the lease or a change to a make-good estimate; Leases where a price index reading is entered on the day the lease starts

A correction to how the calculator carries a right-of-use asset that starts below nil, and to when it holds that asset at nil. Where an incentive received at or before the start of the lease is larger than everything else making up the cost of the asset, the asset genuinely begins below nil. The calculator used to clear that opening amount away in the first period with no entry recording it, so the amount simply disappeared and the schedule no longer agreed with the journals. It is now released evenly across the lease term like any other right-of-use asset, and the journals carry the same release. Separately, the rule that holds the asset at nil now applies only where a reduction in the lease liability is what brings it down; it used to apply to any adjustment, including one that increased the liability, which wrote off part of an asset that should have grown. Leases whose right-of-use asset stays at or above nil are unchanged to the cent. This release also refuses a price index reading entered on the day the lease starts, which the calculator previously discarded, and which could overstate the rent for the rest of the lease.

Under IFRS 16.24 the cost of a right-of-use asset is the initial measurement of the lease liability, plus any lease payments made at or before the start of the lease less any lease incentives received, plus any initial direct costs, plus an estimate of the cost of restoring the asset or the site. Nothing in that paragraph sets a floor, so where the incentive is larger than the rest of the build-up the asset starts below nil. IFRS 16.31 and 16.32 then require the asset to be written down from the start of the lease to the earlier of the end of its useful life and the end of the lease term, and that is what the opening amount now follows: an even release reaching nil at the end of the term, with matching journal entries. Published guidance from BDO Australia addresses this exact case and rejects taking the excess to profit or loss at the start; Grant Thornton reaches the same profit or loss profile through a different presentation. IFRS 16.39 is the paragraph that holds the asset at nil, and it applies only where the carrying amount has already been reduced to nil and there is a further reduction in the measurement of the lease liability, with the remaining amount going to profit or loss. The calculator now reads that condition as written, so an adjustment that increases the liability no longer triggers it. An asset starting below nil is unusual, so the calculator still raises it for review and still asks you to look at the workbook before signing it off. On what the built-in period by period check does and does not cover, stated plainly: it confirms that each period closing balance follows from that period opening balance and the charge, and that an asset which starts a period at or above nil does not end that period below nil. It is not a check on the size of the depreciation charge, and it is not a check on the size of a remeasurement adjustment. Those are covered by the permanent tests that ship with this release, not by the check that runs on your own lease, and nothing here should be read as claiming otherwise. The third change concerns a price index reading dated on the day the lease starts. The calculator sets its own base of 100 at that date, so a reading entered there was discarded and every later reading in the series was then read as a percentage. On a lease of 10,000 a month with a published series of 132.6 at the start and 135.0 six months later, the rent was repriced to 13,500.00 a month instead of 10,181.00, and the pack reported nothing. That entry is now refused, with a message naming the reading and explaining the base, rather than being rebased silently, because choosing between the two readings on your behalf would itself be an invented figure.

E-10 · 2026-07-25engine release 25 July 2026
Affected: Leases that owe an amount at the end of the term, such as a residual value guarantee or a termination penalty, where the lease term is later changed or reassessed and the payments are also linked to an index or a rate

A correction to how the calculator spreads the right-of-use asset over time for leases that owe an amount at the end of the term, such as a residual value guarantee or a termination penalty, where the lease term is later changed and the payments are also linked to an index or a rate. When an index movement was applied after the term had been changed, the calculator went back to the original length of the lease to work out the remaining write-down, instead of using the term now in force. Where the term had been extended, the asset was written down too quickly and reached nil while rent was still owing. Where the term had been shortened, part of the asset was still on the balance sheet on the day the lease ended. Every other lease is unchanged to the cent.

Under IFRS 16.31 and 16.32 the right-of-use asset is written down from the start of the lease to the earlier of the end of the useful life of the asset and the end of the lease term. Where the lessee is not reasonably certain to buy the asset, the useful life does not come into it and the write-down follows the lease term. IFRS 16.42 and 16.43 govern a remeasurement for a change in an index or a rate, and they change the lease liability while leaving the write-down period alone. The calculator already applied that rule when a change of term or a reassessment was processed on its own. It did not apply it on the routes that apply an index movement, so an index movement landing after a change of term reverted to the original length of the lease. The standard does not spell out this combination, so the treatment follows those paragraphs read together. A permanent check now covers every combination of end-of-term amount, direction of the change of term, and position of the index movement, and it carries a control that proves the check can still fail if the fault ever returns.

E-9 · 2026-07-19engine release 19 July 2026
Affected: Leases with a purchase option the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise, where the lease term reaches or passes the end of the asset's useful life; Leases with a termination penalty where you have confirmed the end date is an early exit, which no longer raise the coherence note

A correction to how the calculator depreciates the right-of-use asset for a lease with a purchase option the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise, when the lease term reaches or exceeds the useful life of the underlying asset. Because the lessee is expected to keep and use the asset after the lease ends, the right-of-use asset should be written down over the useful life of the asset, from the start of the lease to the end of that useful life. Previously, when the lease term was as long as or longer than the asset's useful life, the calculator wrote the asset down over the longer lease term instead, so the asset still showed a balance at the point its useful life ended and reached nil only at the later end of the lease. The calculator now writes the asset down over the asset's useful life in this situation, reaching nil at the end of the useful life. For any remaining periods up to the end of the lease the asset is already fully written down, so those periods carry only interest and the lease payment, and the accounting entries still balance. This also applies where a later change to the lease term, or a reassessment of the term, extends the lease past the asset's useful life, because extending the term remeasures the lease liability but does not lengthen the life of the asset. Only leases with a reasonably-certain purchase option whose term reaches or exceeds the asset's useful life are affected; every other lease is unchanged to the cent.

Where a lessee is reasonably certain to exercise a purchase option, the standard requires the right-of-use asset to be depreciated from the start of the lease to the end of the useful life of the underlying asset, on the basis that the lessee expects to keep and use the asset beyond the lease term. The useful life of the asset is a property of the asset, so it is not changed by a later renegotiation of the lease term or by a reassessment of how long the lease will run. A change or reassessment of the term remeasures the lease liability at a revised discount rate, but it does not extend the life of the asset. The calculator applied the correct treatment only when the useful life was longer than the lease term; when the term was as long as, or longer than, the useful life it reverted to spreading the asset over the lease term. On a lease whose term ran past the useful life, this left the asset with a remaining balance at the point the useful life ended, and the asset reached nil only at the later end of the lease; the workbook's own depreciation checks reported the mismatch. The correction spreads the asset over the asset's useful life whether that life is shorter or longer than the lease term. Where the useful life is shorter than the term, the asset reaches nil at the end of the useful life, and the periods after that up to the end of the lease carry only interest and the lease payment, with no further depreciation; the journal entries for those periods still balance, both in total and on each date. Where the useful life is longer than the term, the asset continues to be depreciated past the end of the lease, exactly as before. Only a lease with a reasonably-certain purchase option whose term reaches or exceeds the asset's useful life is affected, including where a later term change or a term reassessment extends the term past the useful life; a lease without such a purchase option, and a lease whose term equals the useful life, are unchanged to the cent. This was found by an independent blind review of an exported workbook. Grounding under the standard: paragraph 16.32 requires depreciation to the end of the underlying asset's useful life where the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise a purchase option, while paragraphs 16.44 and 16.45 treat a change or reassessment of the lease term as a remeasurement of the lease liability rather than a change to the asset's useful life. No published worked example changes, because none of the frozen worked examples is a purchase-option lease whose term reaches or exceeds the asset's useful life; the frozen example set and its recorded fingerprint are unchanged. A saved schedule that is such a lease will change when it is next opened, and the drift advisory in the calculator flags it automatically. The regression check that ships with this correction drives every internal path that chooses the depreciation period, at a term shorter than, equal to, and longer than the useful life, and requires the asset to reach nil at the useful-life point with balanced journals; it includes a control lease without a purchase option that must be unaffected, and a coverage control that fails if any path is left untested. Recorded later, in the same release window: confirming that the end date you entered is an early exit rather than the full contractual end now settles the coherence note raised on a termination-penalty lease, instead of leaving it standing. No figure moves at this point; the confirmation began changing the opening liability in a later release, which is recorded separately. This also reached users under an existing release label rather than a new one, so the load-time advisory treats that label as covering more than one build.

E-8 · 2026-07-18engine release 18 July 2026
Affected: Leases where the make-good or restoration estimate is changed and an amount is also owed at the end of the term; Leases with a termination penalty where the end date is already the full contractual end, which are now told the penalty is not part of the liability

A correction to how the calculator handles a change in a make-good or restoration estimate on a lease that also has an amount due at the end of the term (a residual value guarantee, a purchase-option price the lessee is reasonably certain to pay, or a termination penalty). Previously, recording a restoration estimate change on such a lease left the liability finishing at the full end-of-term amount instead of settling to nil at the end of the lease. The end-of-term amount is now carried through the restoration change unchanged and settles the liability to nil at the lease end, as it already did for every other kind of lease change. Only leases that combine an end-of-term amount with a restoration estimate change are affected; all other leases are unchanged to the cent.

A change in a make-good or restoration estimate is accounted for as a re-estimate of the separate restoration provision, not as a change to the lease liability itself, so the amount due at the end of the lease term stays exactly as it was. On a lease carrying an end-of-term amount, the calculator was correctly carrying that amount through every other kind of subsequent change (a rent renegotiation, a term extension or shortening, an increase or decrease in scope, an index change, and a term reassessment), each of which settled the liability to nil at the end of the lease. The restoration-estimate change was the one path that failed to carry it, so the liability finished stuck at the full end-of-term amount and the internal end-of-term settlement check reported that the liability had not unwound to zero. The correction carries the end-of-term amount through a restoration estimate change unchanged, so it settles the liability to nil at the lease end. Because a restoration estimate change is not a partial termination and does not reduce the scope of the lease, the amount is carried in full and never scaled down. The size of the error was exactly the end-of-term amount on the final period only, with every earlier period identical before and after. This was found by an independent blind review of an exported workbook and confirmed across all three kinds of end-of-term amount and both payment timings. Grounding: under the standard the exercise price of a purchase option the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise, a residual value guarantee, and a penalty for terminating the lease are all part of the lease payments and are therefore settled by the end of the lease term. No worked-example figure that a user could previously have seen on the published examples changes, because none of the frozen worked examples combines an end-of-term amount with a restoration estimate change; the frozen example set is therefore unchanged and its recorded fingerprint is unchanged. A saved schedule that does combine the two will change on next open, and the drift advisory in the calculator flags it automatically. The regression check that ships with this correction runs an end-of-term amount through every kind of subsequent change under both payment timings and requires the liability to settle to nil in each, with a no-end-of-term control that already settled to nil so the check cannot pass vacuously. Recorded later, in the same release window: a lease that carries a termination penalty while its end date is already the full contractual end now raises a coherence note, because on that lease the term does not reflect an early exit and the penalty is therefore not one of the lease payments. No figure moves; what changed is that the situation is pointed out instead of passing without comment. It reached users under this release label rather than a new one, so a lease saved under this label may or may not have had the note, and the load-time advisory now says as much rather than guessing.

E-7 · 2026-07-18engine release 18 July 2026
Affected: Leases where the make-good or restoration estimate is changed, and the rate that change is discounted at

The make-good (restoration or dismantling) provision is now re-measured at the correct discount rate when you change its estimate. When you record a restoration remeasurement (for example the estimated make-good cost changes from 30,000 to 45,000), a new optional field lets you enter the current market-based discount rate for that provision at the remeasurement date. Previously the calculator discounted the revised estimate at the lease's own discount rate, which is not what the standards require: a restoration obligation is a separate IAS 37 provision, and IFRIC 1 with IAS 37 paragraph 47 re-discount it at a current market-based rate at the date of the change, which can differ from the lease rate. On the standard example this moves the remeasured provision from 34,431.05 (discounted at the lease's 5.5%) to 33,626.62 (at a 6% current market rate). The whole change adjusts the right-of-use asset; a decrease that would take the asset below zero is floored at zero with the excess going to profit or loss. If you leave the new rate blank the calculator falls back to the current lease rate as a proxy and shows a clear note asking you to enter the actual current market rate, so a defaulted figure is never silent. Leases that do not carry a restoration remeasurement, or that leave the new rate blank, are unchanged to the cent from before.

When you change the estimated make-good (restoration or dismantling) cost, the revised provision is now discounted at a current market-based rate for that provision rather than at the lease's own discount rate. A make-good obligation is a separate provision under IAS 37 and a component of right-of-use cost (IFRS 16.24(d) and 16.25), not part of the lease liability, so the IFRS 16 discount-rate rules do not govern it; IFRIC 1 (paragraphs 3(b) and 4) with IAS 37 paragraph 47 require a current market-based pre-tax rate at the date of the change, which can differ from the lease rate. A new optional field lets you enter that rate on the make-good remeasurement. On the reference example (an estimate changing from 30,000 to 45,000, effective 1 January 2028, with sixty months remaining), discounting at the lease's 5.5 percent gave 34,431.05, while the required current market rate of 6 percent gives 33,626.62. The whole change adjusts the right-of-use asset (IFRIC 1 paragraph 5(a)); a decrease that would take the asset below zero is floored at zero with the excess going to profit or loss (IFRIC 1 paragraph 5(b), the twin of IFRS 16.39). If you leave the rate blank the calculator falls back to the current lease rate as a disclosed proxy and raises a visible note on the calculator, the export and the saved-lease card asking you to enter the actual current market rate, so a defaulted figure is never silent and the stale original rate is never used. The change is off by default: a lease with no make-good remeasurement, or one that leaves the new rate blank, is unchanged to the cent, and every other modification result is unchanged. Exactly one benchmark scenario stages a make-good remeasurement, so its fingerprint moved (it now carries the new rate and the note) while the other benchmarks are identical; the re-baseline was authorised by an independent comparison that showed no numeric moves, and the benchmark set was re-signed. The engine version is bumped so the saved-lease advisory reaches any user with a make-good remeasurement. The rate on the initial make-good provision at commencement is a separate, larger change and is out of scope for this release.

E-6 · 2026-07-18engine release 18 July 2026
Affected: Short-term and low-value exempt leases carrying an amount the straight-line expense does not include

Completes the previous change (E-5) by closing the whole class: on a short-term or low-value exempt lease, initial direct costs are no longer left out in silence either. The exemption straight-lines only the lease payments, so a cost of obtaining the lease (initial direct costs) is not folded into the expense; but previously it also raised no note, so a workbook carrying a material set-up cost could still certify as ready. It now raises the same action-required note already raised for a residual value guarantee, a termination penalty or a purchase-option price, and the workbook can no longer certify ready until you resolve it. No figure a user could have seen changes — the straight-line expense is unchanged; only the note and the workbook readiness status change.

This completes the previous change by closing the whole class: any figure-bearing input silently dropped on a short-term or low-value exempt lease. The previous entry flagged the two amounts a review happened to hit (a termination penalty and a reasonably-certain purchase-option price). A full enumeration of every figure-bearing input an exempt lease can carry found exactly one remaining silent drop: initial direct costs (IFRS 16.24(c)). Every other figure-bearing input already lands somewhere faithful: absorbed into the straight-line expense (a fixed escalation, a rent-free period, a lease incentive, each a lease payment or a reduction of one), applied as a clean term change or reassessment (which re-spreads the straight-line expense over the revised term), flagged with an action-required note (an index reading, a consideration or scope change, a residual value guarantee, a termination penalty, a low-value purchase-option price, or a make-good provision, none of which has an on-point exempt convention), or blocked (a short-term lease with a reasonably-certain purchase option is a mutual-exclusion error). Variable or turnover rent carries no amount to drop (it is a disclosure flag), and the discount rate is irrelevant on a straight-line-only exempt lease. Initial direct costs had no home because the exempt path opts out of the paragraphs where the cost is added to the right-of-use asset, so a non-zero amount was silently dropped and the total excluded it. It is now flagged with the same action-required note. IFRS grounding (verified 18 July 2026): 16.6 recognises only the lease payments on a straight-line basis, and the lease payments are the components in Appendix A and 16.27 (fixed less incentives, index or rate variable amounts, a residual value guarantee, a purchase-option price, a termination penalty); initial direct costs are not among them. They are a cost of obtaining the lease (16.24(c)), which even the transition guidance (paragraph C10) treats as a discrete, separately-excludable amount, so folding them into the straight-line expense would invent a convention 16.6 does not prescribe and silently move the total. No computed figure changes: the amount is not folded into the expense (the total stays 12,000); only the note and the resulting workbook readiness change. No benchmark covers an exempt lease with initial direct costs, so the benchmark set is unchanged; this is user-facing because workbook readiness flips, so the engine version is bumped.

E-5 · 2026-07-18engine release 18 July 2026
Affected: Short-term and low-value exempt leases carrying an amount the straight-line expense does not include

A short-term or low-value exempt lease that also carried a termination penalty, or a reasonably-certain purchase-option price, no longer leaves that amount out in silence. The exemption straight-lines the payments and has no liability to remeasure, so the calculator does not fold the end-of-term amount into the expense; but previously it also raised no note, so a workbook carrying a material penalty could still certify as ready. It now raises the same action-required note it already raised for a residual value guarantee, and the workbook can no longer certify ready until you resolve it. No figure a user could have seen changes — the straight-line expense is unchanged; only the note and the workbook readiness status change (they now correctly refuse to sign off over an unadjusted figure).

A short-term or low-value exempt lease that also carried a termination penalty (IFRS 16.27(e)) or a reasonably-certain purchase-option exercise price (IFRS 16.27(d)) previously left that amount out with no note, so a workbook carrying a material amount could still certify as ready. The exemption straight-lines the payments (IFRS 16.5 to 16.6) and has no liability to remeasure, so the amount is not folded into the expense; but it must be surfaced. The calculator already raised an action-required note for a residual value guarantee on an exempt lease, so the mechanism existed; these two amounts were simply not among the events it enumerated. They are now, so the workbook can no longer certify as ready until you resolve the note. For the purchase option this applies to a low-value exempt lease, because a short-term exemption held together with a reasonably-certain purchase option is already a blocking mutual-exclusion error and must not be double-signalled. No computed figure changes: an exempt lease carries no schedule and the amount is not folded into the straight-line expense (a ten-period lease at 1,200 stays at 12,000, and the low-value purchase-option case stays at 12,000); only the note and the resulting workbook readiness change. No benchmark covers an exempt lease with a termination penalty or a purchase option, so the benchmark set is unchanged. This is user-facing because the workbook readiness a user sees flips, so the engine version is bumped and the saved-lease advisory reaches any affected user.

E-4 · 2026-07-18engine release 18 July 2026
Affected: Leases shortened by a change that also owe an amount at the end of the term; Leases with more than one change, reduced in scope, that also owe an amount at the end of the term

A correction to how an end-of-term amount (a residual value guarantee, a purchase-option exercise price or a termination penalty) is measured when a modification shortens the lease term. Previously, on certain term-shortening modifications the liability schedule finished with a small negative balance at the revised lease end (from a few cents up to about 2,450 currency units on the affected test cases) instead of unwinding exactly to zero, because the end-of-term amount was discounted over a slightly longer horizon than the schedule actually ran. The end-of-term amount is now discounted over exactly the same remaining time the schedule uses, so the liability unwinds to zero at the revised lease end by construction. Only leases that combine an end-of-term amount with a term-shortening modification (or a modification stack that reduces the scope) are affected; all other leases are unchanged to the cent.

On certain term-shortening modifications the liability schedule finished with a small negative balance at the revised lease end, from a few cents up to about 2,450 currency units on the affected cases, instead of unwinding exactly to zero. The cause was that the end-of-term amount, a residual value guarantee, a purchase-option exercise price or a termination penalty, was discounted over a slightly longer remaining horizon than the schedule itself ran: when a term-shortening leaves a partial final period (less than a whole month), the discount horizon was counted in whole periods while the schedule accretes over the actual month-fractions, so the amount came in a little too small and the full booking at the final period left a negative residue. The end-of-term amount is now discounted over exactly the same remaining time the schedule uses, so the liability unwinds to zero at the revised lease end by construction, and the modification working carries the same corrected figure so it still reconciles to the schedule. The amount settles at the end of the final period, after that period's full interest, under both payment timings. The result is unchanged to the cent wherever every remaining period is a full month, so the base, index, reassessment and clean-boundary modification paths are unaffected. IFRS grounding: 16.27(c), (d) and (e) (the amount is part of the lease payments), 16.45 (revised-rate remeasurement of the revised payments) and 16.46(a) (a term-shortening derecognition leaves the surviving liability to unwind to exactly zero at the revised end); the amount is still carried forward in full, which this fix does not change, it corrects only the discount horizon.
